findings.title: October 2026 Patch Tuesday: 1,413 CVEs Include Three Zero-Days and 75 Critical Vulnerabilities
Echo static file middleware route protection bypass via encoded dot-dot traversal
findings.summary:
## Summary

Echo v5.2.0 contains a bypass of the fix for GHSA-vfp3-v2gw-7wfq. The fix rejects encoded path separators such as `%2F` and `%5C` before static file path unescaping, but two traversal forms still bypass route-level middleware protections for static files.

The primary bypass uses encoded dot-dot segments. A request such as `/public/%2E%2E/admin/secret.txt` passes the encoded-separator guard, is unescaped to `public/../admin/secret.txt`, then `path.Clean` resolves it to `admin/secret.txt`. If `/admin/*` is protected by middleware but the static filesystem is mounted at `/`, the protected file is returned through the public static route.

A second bypass exists when `UseEscapedPathForMatching=true`. In that mode, the router normalizes encoded separators before the static handler checks the wildcard. The handler receives a decoded wildcard with no `%` characters, so the encoded-separator guard does not run on the original encoded path.

## Impact

An unauthenticated attacker can read files that an application intended to protect with route-level middleware, when those files are also reachable through a static filesystem mount after path normalization.

The high-severity variant works with the default router configuration and requires only encoded dot-dot path segments. The direct protected route returns 403, while the public static route returns the protected file content.

The `UseEscapedPathForMatching=true` variant is lower severity because it requires a non-default router configuration.

## Affected versions

Tested vulnerable:

- `github.com/labstack/echo/v5` v5.2.0
- Current `master` at `5786024ea4d85c01784796e8aa7aac53e007b39b`

No patched version is currently known.


## Policy and version checks

GitHub Private Vulnerability Reporting is enabled for `labstack/echo`. The repository has a root `SECURITY.md` and accepts security reports through GitHub Security Advisories.

The vulnerable code was revalidated on both current `master` and the latest rel

findings.summary: Posted by Thomas Brunner, Yu-Han Liu, Moni Pande At Google, our Threat Intelligence teams are dedicated to staying ahead of real-world adversarial activity, proactively monitoring emerging threats before they can impact users. Right now, Indirect Prompt Injection (IPI) is a top priority for the security community, anticipating it as a primary attack vector for adversaries to target and compromise AI agents. But while the danger of IPI is widely discussed, are threat actors actually exploiting this vector today – and if so, how? To answer these questions and to uncover real-world abuse, we initiated a broad sweep of the public web to monitor for known indirect prompt injection patterns. This is what we found. The threat of indirect prompt injection Unlike a direct injection where a user "jailbreaks" a chatbot, IPI occurs when an AI system processes content—like a website, email, or document—that contains malicious instructions. When the AI reads this poisoned content, it may silently follow the attacker's commands instead of the user's original intent. This is not a new area of concern for us and Google has been working tirelessly to combat these threats. Our efforts involve cross-functional collaboration between researchers at Google DeepMind (GDM) and defenders like the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG). We have previously detailed our work in this area and researchers have further highlighted the evolving nature of these vulnerabilities. Despite this collective focus, a fundamental question remains: to what degree are real-world malicious actors currently operationalizing these attacks? Proactive monitoring at Google The landscape of IPI on the web There are many channels through which attackers might try to send prompt injections. However, one location is particularly easy to observe - the public web. Here, threat actors may simply seed prompt injections on websites in hope of corrupting AI systems that browse them. findings.title: Google Workspace’s continuous approach to mitigating indirect prompt injections
findings.summary: Posted by Adam Gavish, Google GenAI Security Team Indirect prompt injection (IPI) is an evolving threat vector targeting users of complex AI applications with multiple data sources, such as Workspace with Gemini. This technique enables the attacker to influence the behavior of an LLM by injecting malicious instructions into the data or tools used by the LLM as it completes the user’s query. This may even be possible without any input directly from the user. IPI is not the kind of technical problem you “solve” and move on. Sophisticated LLMs with increasing use of agentic automation combined with a wide range of content create an ultra-dynamic and evolving playground for adversarial attacks. That’s why Google takes a sophisticated and comprehensive approach to these attacks. We’re continuously improving LLM resistance to IPI attacks and launching AI application capabilities with ever-improving defenses. Staying ahead of the latest indirect prompt injection attacks is critical to our mission of securing Workspace with Gemini. findings.title: Architecting Security for Agentic Capabilities in Chrome
findings.summary: Posted by Nathan Parker, Chrome security team Chrome has been advancing the web’s security for well over 15 years, and we’re committed to meeting new challenges and opportunities with AI. Billions of people trust Chrome to keep them safe by default, and this is a responsibility we take seriously. Following the recent launch of Gemini in Chrome and the preview of agentic capabilities , we want to share our approach and some new innovations to improve the safety of agentic browsing. The primary new threat facing all agentic browsers is indirect prompt injection . It can appear in malicious sites, third-party content in iframes, or from user-generated content like user reviews, and can cause the agent to take unwanted actions such as initiating financial transactions or exfiltrating sensitive data. Given this open challenge, we are investing in a layered defense that includes both deterministic and probabilistic defenses to make it difficult and costly for attackers to cause harm. Designing safe agentic browsing for Chrome has involved deep collaboration of security experts across Google. We built on Gemini's existing protections and agent security principles and have implemented several new layers for Chrome. We’re introducing a user alignment critic where the agent’s actions are vetted by a separate model that is isolated from untrusted content. We’re also extending Chrome’s origin-isolation capabilities to constrain what origins the agent can interact with, to just those that are relevant to the task. Our layered defense also includes user confirmations for critical steps, real-time detection of threats , and red-teaming and response . We’ll step through these layers below. findings.summary: Posted by Jeff Vander Stoep, Android Last year, we wrote about why a memory safety strategy that focuses on vulnerability prevention in new code quickly yields durable and compounding gains. This year we look at how this approach isn’t just fixing things, but helping us move faster . This data covers first-party and third-party (open source) code changes to the Android platform across C, C++, Java, Kotlin, and Rust. This post is published a couple of months before the end of 2025, but Android’s industry-standard 90-day patch window means that these results are very likely close to final. We can and will accelerate patching when necessary. We adopted Rust for its security and are seeing a 1000x reduction in memory safety vulnerability density compared to Android’s C and C++ code . But the biggest surprise was Rust's impact on software delivery. findings.title: Mitigating prompt injection attacks with a layered defense strategy
findings.summary: Posted by Adam Gavish, Google GenAI Security Team With the rapid adoption of generative AI, a new wave of threats is emerging across the industry with the aim of manipulating the AI systems themselves. One such emerging attack vector is indirect prompt injections. Unlike direct prompt injections, where an attacker directly inputs malicious commands into a prompt, indirect prompt injections involve hidden malicious instructions within external data sources. These may include emails, documents, or calendar invites that instruct AI to exfiltrate user data or execute other rogue actions. As more governments, businesses, and individuals adopt generative AI to get more done, this subtle yet potentially potent attack becomes increasingly pertinent across the industry, demanding immediate attention and robust security measures. At Google, our teams have a longstanding precedent of investing in a defense-in-depth strategy, including robust evaluation, threat analysis, AI security best practices , AI red-teaming , adversarial training, and model hardening for generative AI tools. This approach enables safer adoption of Gemini in Google Workspace and the Gemini app (we refer to both in this blog as “Gemini” for simplicity). Below we describe our prompt injection mitigation product strategy based on extensive research, development, and deployment of improved security mitigations. A layered security approach Google has taken a layered security approach introducing security measures designed for each stage of the prompt lifecycle. From Gemini 2.5 model hardening, to purpose-built machine learning (ML) models detecting malicious instructions, to system-level safeguards, we are meaningfully elevating the difficulty, expense, and complexity faced by an attacker. This approach compels adversaries to resort to methods that are either more easily identified or demand greater resources. findings.summary: Russian State-Supported Cyber Actors Conduct Phishing Campaign Targeting Users of Zimbra Collaboration Suite Executive summary A group of Russian state-supported cyber actors has been targeting and compromising various Western government and commercial organizations using the Zimbra Collaboration Suite (ZCS) software since at least July 2025. The Russian state-supported advanced persistent threat (APT) group’s activity is tracked in the cybersecurity community under several names (see Cybersecurity industry tracking ), primarily as “LAUNDRY BEAR,” a name initially coined by the Netherlands General Intelligence and Security Service (AIVD) and Defence Intelligence and Security Service (MIVD) [ 1 ]. LAUNDRY BEAR’s targeting is almost certainly to gather sensitive information for the Russian Federation, with these actors primarily focusing on the covert acquisition of email data. Previous campaigns indicated LAUNDRY BEAR relied on unsophisticated initial access techniques—including password spraying, phishing, and pass-the-cookie—allowing the group to successfully run high-volume operations. The latest campaign targeting ZCS uses a novel exploit that was a zero-day vulnerability when first exploited and continues to be successfully exploited. The vulnerability, Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) CVE-2025-66376 , was patched in November 2025. This demonstrates LAUNDRY BEAR’s intent and ability to deploy increasingly sophisticated technical capabilities. Unlike traditional phishing campaigns that persuade a user into taking an action, such as clicking a link or opening a file, LAUNDRY BEAR’s latest campaign leverages a view-based exploit that only requires a user to view a malicious email within a vulnerable version of the webmail service. findings.title: Electrum: Malicious server can replace a just-broadcast tx and try to trick user into RBF-ing it
findings.summary:
### Summary

The main Electrum server the client connects to is trusted with mempool ("unconfirmed") transactions. This is documented [design](https://electrum.readthedocs.io/en/latest/faq.html#does-electrum-trust-servers). [0]

However now someone figured out a way to practically exploit it:
- when the client broadcasts a new tx1, a malicious server can swallow it,
- and update the client's history with a conflicting (invalid) tx2 that replaces the outputs with the attacker's output address.
- Tx2 has invalid signatures, but this is not checked (due to light client design).
- The wallet will display tx2 as an unconfirmed transaction - tx1 will not be displayed.
- If the client then manually RBF fee-bumps tx2, the client will sign it with a higher fee, and hence pay the attacker.

### Fixes

Commit 90fe30822 contains the fix [1], included in version 4.8.3.
The client now verifies the signatures of `wallet.is_mine` inputs for mempool txs (before adding them to its local history).

Users should upgrade (and regularly do so in any case).
As a workaround, without upgrading, when signing any transaction, for bumping the fee or not, they should verify the output addresses and amounts are as expected.

Clients that connect to servers they trust (e.g. run their own) are not affected.


### Remarks

- some servers are performing this attack in the wild
- electrum received two user-reports of this. user1 noticed after broadcasting tx1 the wallet history contained a different tx. user2 bumped the fee of tx2 and lost money.
- user1 reported tx1 was not propagated over the bitcoin p2p, so the server held it
- both reported the attacker's output address in tx2 was grinded to match the last four chars of the legit address from tx1
- based on user2's report, the server constructed a tx2 with zero fee (presumably in hope of the user bumping its fee)
- even with the fix, we still only validate "is_mine" inputs (i.e. paying from addresses that the wallet owns). So e.g. "incoming" txs

findings.title: Mem0: Cross-tenant conversation leak via unescaped delimiter collision in session-scope key (_build_session_scope)
findings.summary:
Summary

_build_session_scope() in mem0/memory/main.py builds the conversation-history scope key used to fetch/store the last N raw messages by naively joining caller-supplied user_id/agent_id/run_id values with unescaped & and = delimiters:

def _build_session_scope(filters):
    parts = []
    for key in sorted(["user_id", "agent_id", "run_id"]):
        val = filters.get(key)
        if val:
            parts.append(f"{key}={val}")
    return "&".join(parts)

_validate_and_trim_entity_id() (the only validation applied to these values) rejects only empty/whitespace-only strings — it never forbids & or =. This scope string is then used as an exact-match key against a SQLite column (storage.py: WHERE session_scope = ?) to fetch the last 10 raw messages for a given scope (main.py, Phase 0 of _add_to_vector_store, both sync and async).

Impact

Any caller who controls only their own run_id (or agent_id) — a very common integration shape, since apps frequently pass a client-/session-supplied identifier straight through as run_id without namespacing — can craft a value containing &user_id=<victim> (or &agent_id=<victim>) that produces a scope string byte-for-byte identical to a different tenant's real scope string.

Concretely: Tenant A calls add(msgs, user_id="alice", run_id="proj-x") → scope "run_id=proj-x&user_id=alice". An attacker who can only set run_id calls add(msgs, run_id="proj-x&user_id=alice") → identical scope string. The attacker's next add() call:

1. Reads Tenant A's raw prior conversation via get_last_messages(session_scope) and splices it verbatim into the attacker's own LLM fact-extraction prompt — a direct cross-tenant confidentiality leak (conversation content, potentially including PII, credentials, etc.).
2. Writes into the same colliding row-set via save_messages(), whose eviction logic (DELETE FROM messages WHERE session_scope = ? AND id NOT IN (...)) can evict/interleave Tenant A's history — permanent cross-tenant data corruption, not just a re

findings.title: vLLM: Permissive default CORS origins allow cross-origin requests to the vLLM HTTP server
findings.summary:
### Summary

The OpenAI-compatible server registers Starlette `CORSMiddleware` with
`allowed_origins` defaulting to `["*"]`, and performs no authentication unless
`--api-key` (or `VLLM_API_KEY`) is configured. A web page on any origin can send
requests to a vLLM server that the victim's browser can reach (for example
`localhost` or an internal/VPN address) and read the responses. The default
`allow_credentials=False` blocks cookie-bearing cross-origin requests; because
vLLM authenticates with a bearer header rather than cookies, the wildcard still
permits untokenized access to an unauthenticated server and read access when the
caller already holds a token.

### Details

Affected components

- `vllm/entrypoints/launchers/cli_args.py` - `allowed_origins` default value.
- `vllm/entrypoints/serve/middleware/register.py` - `CORSMiddleware`
  registration.
- `vllm/entrypoints/serve/middleware/authenticate.py` - auth middleware and its
  guarded path prefixes.

 Root cause

`vllm/entrypoints/launchers/cli_args.py`:

```python
allow_credentials: bool = False
"""Allow credentials."""
allowed_origins: list[str] = field(default_factory=lambda: ["*"])
"""Allowed origins."""
```

`vllm/entrypoints/serve/middleware/register.py`:

```python
app.add_middleware(
    CORSMiddleware,
    allow_origins=args.allowed_origins,
    allow_credentials=args.allow_credentials,
    allow_methods=args.allowed_methods,
    allow_headers=args.allowed_headers,
)
```

The auth middleware is added only when a token is configured and guards only the
`/v1`, `/v2`, `/inference`, and `/cohere` prefixes. `/v1/load_lora_adapter` and
`/v1/unload_lora_adapter` are inside `/v1` and therefore do require a key when
one is set; they are open only when no key is configured and dynamic LoRA
updating is enabled.

### Impact


- A malicious page can enumerate models (`GET /v1/models`), issue
  `POST /v1/chat/completions`, consume GPU time, and read model output through

findings.title: vLLM: DoS via unbounded chat_template Jinja2 rendering exhausts the renderer thread pool
findings.summary:
### Summary
vLLM renders chat templates by passing the resolved Jinja2 source to `tokenizer.apply_chat_template()`, which compiles and `.render()`s it in an `ImmutableSandboxedEnvironment`. The sandbox prevents code-execution escapes but imposes **no wall-clock timeout, no output-size cap, and no nested-loop or binop limit**. The render runs in a `ThreadPoolExecutor` whose `max_workers` defaults to **1**, and CPython worker threads cannot be interrupted. An authenticated API client (or a malicious model repo loaded with `trust_remote_code=False`) can therefore submit a single short template and permanently wedge **all** chat-style endpoints (`/v1/chat/completions`, `/v1/responses`, `/tokenize`, `/pooling`-chat, `/invocations`-chat) for every tenant until the process is restarted. A string-multiplication variant instead OOM-kills the API-server process. Because of a separately-reported (GHSA-jmjw-q4x3-hmc2) gate omission on `/v1/responses`, the remote authenticated attacker vector works in **default `vllm serve` configuration** with no operator opt-in.

### Impact
A single authenticated request of <100 bytes permanently denies all chat-style inference (`/v1/chat/completions`, `/v1/responses`, `/tokenize`, `/pooling`-chat, `/invocations`-chat) to **every tenant** of the API-server replica until the operator restarts the process. The string-multiplication variant OOM-kills the process. In a multi-tenant deployment this is a cross-tenant denial-of-service from any one tenant. From the malicious-model angle, a model repo whose `tokenizer_config.json` carries the hostile template wedges every replica that loads it on the first legitimate chat request, with `trust_remote_code=False`.

**Preconditions:** any non-harmony model (`model_type != gpt_oss`); `renderer_num_workers` at its default of 1; for the default-config authenticated API attacker vector, `--chat-template` must be unset (the default because most HF models ship their own).

findings.title: Go JOSE: Panic during CBC-HMAC processing
findings.summary:
### Summary

Decrypting a ciphertext with "A128CBC-HS256", "A192CBC-HS384", or "A256CBC-HS512" can result in a panic on untrusted input.

Note this advisory is the same as https://github.com/go-jose/go-jose/security/advisories/GHSA-6mp9-8xrw-74r4.

### Details

Insufficient validation of parameters can lead to attempting to index into an empty buffer. See https://github.com/go-jose/go-jose/pull/292.

### Workarounds

If the application does not require the CBC-HMAC modes for content encryption, and is using github.com/go-jose/go-jose/v4, do not include them in the list of ContentEncryption algorithms passed to ParseEncrypted / ParseEncryptedJSON / ParseEncryptedCompact.

### Impact

Denial of service vulnerability. Any application which decrypts untrusted ciphertexts with the indicated algorithms is affected.

### Acknowledgements

Thanks to Joshua Rogers of AISLE Research for reporting this problem.

graphql-scalars PhoneNumber scalar is vulnerable to regular expression denial of service
findings.summary:
## Summary

The regular expression behind `GraphQLPhoneNumber` since 1.24.1 backtracks exponentially. A string made of a run of digits followed by one character that makes the match fail (for example `"1".repeat(30) + "x"`) blocks the JavaScript thread for seconds, and every additional digit doubles the time.

graphql-js calls `parseLiteral` while *validating* a document and `parseValue` while coercing variables, so the regex runs for every request that merely contains such a value in a `PhoneNumber` position, before execution and before any authentication or authorization step of the server. One small unauthenticated request is enough to stall a server process.

## Affected versions

- `graphql-scalars` >= 1.24.1, <= 2.0.0 (2.0.0 is the current `latest`; the default branch still has the same pattern).
- Not affected: 1.24.0 and the earlier versions I checked (1.22.4, 1.23.0), which use the linear `/^\+[1-9]\d{6,14}$/`.
- Introduced by #2719 (c7f58da16, "PhoneNumber scalar is not fully compatible with E.164 format so updated regex to support phone number with extension"), released as 1.24.1 on 2025-01-29.

The payload was ran against 1.22.4, 1.23.0, 1.24.0, 1.24.1, 1.24.2, 1.25.0, 1.26.0 and 2.0.0: the first three reject it instantly, the other five show the exponential growth.

## Root cause

`src/scalars/PhoneNumber.ts`:

```js
const PHONE_NUMBER_REGEX = /^\+?\d{1,3}(\-|\x20)?\(?\d+\)?((\-|\x20)?\d+)+$/;
```

In `\d+\)?((\-|\x20)?\d+)+$` the separator is optional, so a run of n digits can be split across the inner `\d+` and the outer `+` iterations in a number of ways that is exponential in n. When the overall match fails, for instance on a trailing non-digit, the engine tries all of them.

## Proof of concept

1. The scalar alone (`npm i graphql graphql-scalars@2.0.0`):

```js
import { GraphQLPhoneNumber } from 'graphql-scalars';

for (const ok of ['+41791234567', '079 123 45 67', '+1 (123) 456-7890', 'nope']) {
  try { GraphQLPhoneNumber.parseValue(ok); } catch

findings.title: Autobahn Python: permessage-brotli inflates a whole frame before maxMessagePayloadSize is checked (incomplete fix of GHSA-hxp9-w8x3-p566)
findings.summary:
### Summary

permessage-brotli inflates each frame fully before checking maxMessagePayloadSize, so one 421-byte frame makes the server allocate about 545 MiB even with a 1 MiB message limit (brotli expands about 1,000,000:1). Any unauthenticated client can exhaust server memory this way on servers that enable permessage-brotli. This bypasses the GHSA-hxp9-w8x3-p566 fix.

### Details

In 26.7.1 the receive path passes the remaining `maxMessagePayloadSize` budget to `decompress_message_data(..., max_output_len=...)`. deflate and bzip2 stop at that budget. `PerMessageBrotli.decompress_message_data` (`compress_brotli.py`) instead calls `self._decompressor.process(data)` with no limit and compares the length afterwards, so the whole frame is inflated first.

The code comment and changelog say this is still "bounded on the wire by `maxFramePayloadSize`", but brotli reaches about 1,000,000:1 (841 bytes inflate to 1 GiB), so that bound means little. A 421-byte frame against a 1 MiB budget peaks at 545 MiB before the 1009 rejection.

An autobahn asyncio server on 127.0.0.1 accepting permessage-brotli, with `maxFramePayloadSize=64 KiB` and `maxMessagePayloadSize=1 MiB`, received one small brotli frame from an autobahn client and peaked at 545 MiB (baseline 28 MiB). A few concurrent connections can exhaust memory.

brotli ≥ 1.2.0 has `Decompressor.process(data, output_buffer_limit=N)`, so the backend can stop at `max_output_len` like deflate and bzip2 (and the extra's floor can be raised to `brotli>=1.2.0`).

Tested on autobahn 26.7.1 (latest) with brotli 1.2.0; `compress_brotli.py` on master is unchanged. This affects servers that enable permessage-brotli (opt-in, needs the `compress` extra).

How to run the PoC
```
python3 -m venv venv && . venv/bin/activate
pip install autobahn==26.7.1 brotli==1.2.0
python3 poc_autobahn.py
```

findings.title: zip: Critical Parser Differential & Security Control Bypass via Dual-Header Inconsistencies (Zip Cloaking) Leading to Arbitrary File Overwrite & RCE
findings.summary:
## Summary
A critical architectural parser differential exists in the `zip` crate (`<= 9.0.4`) between random-access archive readers (`ZipArchive`) and streaming readers (`ZipStreamReader`). `ZipArchive` considers the Central Directory File Header (CDFH) authoritative and ignores the filename declared in the Local File Header (LFH). In contrast, `ZipStreamReader` relies exclusively on the Local File Header (LFH) when extracting files to the filesystem.

This discrepancy enables ZIP archives to appear to have different file paths and contents according to which tool is reading them.

---

## Details

### Architectural Root Cause
In the PKWARE ZIP archive format, every file entry is defined in two distinct locations:
1. **Local File Header (LFH):** Precedes the compressed payload of each file in the body of the archive.
2. **Central Directory File Header (CDFH):** Stored in a contiguous index at the end of the archive.

In `zip2`:
- `src/read/zip_archive.rs`: `ZipArchive` parses the central directory into `SharedBuilder.files`. All file lookups by index or name read exclusively from the CDFH table, completely ignoring the filename present in the LFH.
- `src/read/stream.rs:L86-L141`: `ZipStreamReader::visit` and `ZipStreamReader::extract` read sequentially from the stream without verifying the central directory index. Each entry is parsed via `read_zipfile_from_stream` and written to disk using the unverified filename declared in the LFH:
  ```rust
  // src/read/stream.rs
  fn visit_file<R: Read>(&mut self, file: &mut ZipFile<'_, R>) -> ZipResult<()> {
      file.safe_prepare_path(&self.outpath, &mut outpath, None::<&(_, fn(&Path) -> bool)>)?;
      let mut outfile = fs::File::create(&outpath)?;
      io::copy(file, &mut outfile)?;
      Ok(())
  }
  ```
- `src/write.rs:L1552`: The crate explicitly exposes `shallow_copy_file`, an API that constructs dual-header desynchronizations by adding a new CDFH entry with an alias name pointing to an existing file without updatin

findings.title: LangGraph JavaScript custom authentication may permit cross-user Store access
findings.summary:
## Summary

LangGraph deployments using JavaScript or TypeScript custom authentication may fail to apply Store authorization changes returned by an authorization handler. In affected deployments, an authenticated user may be able to access Store data outside their authorized namespace.

## Required conditions

A deployment is affected only when all of the following conditions apply:

- It uses an affected `langgraph-api` version.
- It runs JavaScript or TypeScript custom authentication.
- Its Store authorization handler relies on rewriting the requested namespace to restrict each user to their own data.
- The attacker can authenticate as an ordinary user.
- Multiple users' data is stored through the affected authorization path.

Python custom authentication handlers are not affected. JavaScript or TypeScript handlers that reject unauthorized namespace requests instead of rewriting them are also not affected.

The attack does not require administrator privileges, user interaction, a race condition, or the bypass of another mitigation.

## Impact

An authenticated user may be able to read, overwrite, search, or delete Store data belonging to another user.

## Patches

The issue is fixed in `langgraph-api` version `0.15.0`. The server now carries changes made by a JavaScript or TypeScript authorization handler across the runtime boundary and applies them before performing the Store operation. It validates the resulting namespace after authorization and rejects the request if an authorization change is malformed or cannot be applied safely.

Users should upgrade to `langgraph-api>=0.15.0`.

## Workarounds

Deployments that cannot upgrade immediately should change JavaScript or TypeScript Store authorization handlers to reject requests for unauthorized namespaces rather than relying on namespace rewriting.

This workaround must be applied to every Store action exposed by the deployment.

When that directory already exists they adopt it after checking only that it is a real directory, not who owns it. findings.title: filelock: SoftFileLock removes a live holder's marker when another user forges the PID in a writable marker
findings.summary:
`SoftFileLock`, `MarkerSoftFileLock`, `SoftFileLease`, their async variants and a `FileLock` that has fallen back to a soft lock on `ENOSYS` decide from the record inside the marker file whether its owner is gone. The marker is the file whose presence says a process holds the lock. They do not check who could have written that record.

A local user who can write the marker but cannot remove it rewrites the holder's record to name a dead PID (process id). `StrictSoftFileLock` and `AsyncStrictSoftFileLock` check `<path>.filelock` (the coordination directory that holds the lock's state) with one `lstat` call on its name. `lstat` reports what a name is without following a symbolic link (a file that redirects to another path). findings.title: Echo has a Static Middleware Double-Unescape Path Traversal
findings.summary:
## Summary

Commit a9ede66a (PR #3006, issue #2599) silently fixed a path traversal vulnerability in the Echo web framework's static file middleware.

## Vulnerability

The static middleware double-unescaped URL paths. Go's net/http already decodes Request.URL.Path, but middleware/static.go unconditionally called url.PathUnescape() again:

```go
// BEFORE (vulnerable)
pathUnescape := true
```

This reassembled path traversal sequences from double-encoded input. An attacker could send GET /%2e%2e%2fsecret.txt or /..%252fsecret.txt and the double-unescape would produce ../secret.txt.

## Fix
```go
// AFTER (fixed)
pathUnescape := false
```

The commit's test TestStatic_percentEncodedTraversalIsBlocked explicitly verifies traversal vectors are blocked.

## Impact
Arbitrary file read from server filesystem via percent-encoded path traversal.

## References
- Fix: https://github.com/labstack/echo/commit/a9ede66a
- Issue: https://github.com/labstack/echo/issues/2599
- PR: https://github.com/labstack/echo/pull/3006

## Patches

Fixed in `github.com/labstack/echo/v5` v5.2.0 and `github.com/labstack/echo/v4` v4.15.3, where the Static middleware stopped unescaping an already decoded path. Maintainer analysis: reading files outside the configured root could not be reproduced; the confirmed impact was that a double-encoded slash (`%252F`) could reach a file under a guarded route when the Static middleware is registered globally. Upgrade to v5.4.0 / v4.16.0 or later, which also includes related fixes for encoded and dot-segment paths.

## Workarounds

Keep files that need protection outside the Static middleware's root directory.

findings.title: Echo's middleware.Static: `%2F`-encoded path bypasses route/group middleware guarding a statically-served path
findings.summary:
## Summary

When `middleware.Static` is mounted globally (`e.Use(middleware.Static(...))`) and an application relies on a **route- or group-level middleware guard** to restrict a path that also falls under the served static root, a `%2F`-encoded request bypasses that guard while the file is still served. This is the same encoding/decoding mismatch fixed for `StaticFS`/`StaticDirectoryHandler` in CVE-2026-55677 / GHSA-vfp3-v2gw-7wfq, but the fix did not cover the `middleware.Static` path. In addition, the `StaticConfig.EnablePathUnescaping` docstring states the default configuration prevents exactly this bypass, which is inaccurate for the global-mount case.

**This is not path traversal:** no file outside the static root is accessed. The served file lives inside the static root; the issue is that access-control expectations set by a route guard are inconsistent between the literal and `%2F`-encoded forms of the same path.

## Details

Root cause — the router and the static handler disagree on how to interpret `%2F`:

- The router matches routes on the **raw, still-encoded** path, so `GET /admin%2Fsecret.txt` does **not** match a `/admin/...` route or group; any middleware attached to that route/group is therefore skipped.
- `middleware.Static` selects its path source in `middleware/static.go` (~L219): with a global `e.Use` mount there is no wildcard route, so it uses `c.Request().URL.Path`, which `net/http` has already **decoded** (`%2F` → `/`). It then `path.Clean`s (~L235) and `Open`s (~L259) `admin/secret.txt`, serving the file.

Net effect: for the literal path the guard runs; for the `%2F`-encoded path the guard is skipped but the same file is served.

Relevant code:
- `middleware/static.go` ~L219 (`p := c.Request().URL.Path`), ~L235 (`path.Clean`), ~L259 (`currentFS.Open`)
- `StaticConfig.EnablePathUnescaping` docstring (`static.go` ~L60-67) — claims the default prevents the `/admin%2fprivate.txt` → `/admin/*` guard bypass; this is not true for the global moun

findings.title: Bringing Rust to the Pixel Baseband
findings.summary: Posted by Jiacheng Lu, Software Engineer, Google Pixel Team Google is continuously advancing the security of Pixel devices. We have been focusing on hardening the cellular baseband modem against exploitation. Recognizing the risks associated within the complex modem firmware, Pixel 9 shipped with mitigations against a range of memory-safety vulnerabilities. For Pixel 10, Google is advancing its proactive security measures further. Following our previous discussion on "Deploying Rust in Existing Firmware Codebases" , this post shares a concrete application: integrating a memory-safe Rust DNS(Domain Name System) parser into the modem firmware. The new Rust-based DNS parser significantly reduces our security risk by mitigating an entire class of vulnerabilities in a risky area, while also laying the foundation for broader adoption of memory-safe code in other areas. Here we share our experience of working on it, and hope it can inspire the use of more memory safe languages in low-level environments. Why Modem Memory Safety Can’t Wait In recent years, we have seen increasing interest in the cellular modem from attackers and security researchers. For example, Google's Project Zero gained remote code execution on Pixel modems over the Internet. Pixel modem has tens of Megabytes of executable code. Given the complexity and remote attack surface of the modem, other critical memory safety vulnerabilities may remain in the predominantly memory-unsafe firmware code. Why DNS? The DNS protocol is most commonly known in the context of browsers finding websites. With the evolution of cellular technology, modern cellular communications have migrated to digital data networks; consequently, even basic operations such as call forwarding rely on DNS services. DNS is a complex protocol and requires parsing of untrusted data, which can lead to vulnerabilities, particularly when implemented in a memory-unsafe language (example: CVE-2024-27227 ).
